title: Battle of Dabu-dong (1950): The Stand at the Pusan Perimeter
subtitle: Aug 1 – Sep 24, 1950

lines: August 1950. Dabu-dong, North Gyeongsang Province.
From here, the city of Taegu lay barely twenty kilometers away.
The North Koreans were certain.
"Cross this pass, and Taegu is ours."
s02.label: Dramatization

lines: For more than a month since the war began, the ROK Army had known only defeat and retreat.
This time, the outcome seemed already decided.
s02b.label: Troops on the move (Aug 1950)

lines: If Taegu fell, the entire Naktong line would collapse.
And after that... Pusan, and the sea.
Holding this final gate were the ROK 1st Division and the U.S. 27th Infantry Regiment.
They were outnumbered more than two to one.
Yet fifty-five days later,
it was the North Korean army that broke.
s05.text:
Fifty-five days later,
the road to Taegu was still closed

lines: Where hilltops changed hands several times a day,
and tanks traded fire through the night in the valley below.
This is the story of the last line on the Naktong: the Battle of Dabu-dong.
s06.title: Battle of Dabu-dong
s06.sub: The Stand at the Pusan Perimeter · 1950

lines: June 25th, 1950. One month into the war,
ROK and UN forces had been pushed south without pause.
By early August, all that remained was a small corner in the southeast of the peninsula.
A line drawn along the Naktong River: the Pusan Perimeter.
To break it, the North Koreans drove five divisions toward Taegu.
And the tip of that spear pointed at Dabu-dong.
In early August, the ROK 1st Division first held the Naktong riverbank for nine days, blocking every crossing.
Then, on August 12th, it moved to a new front: Dabu-dong.
Why Dabu-dong?
Because the main road from Sangju to Taegu funnels into this one narrow valley.
To the west, Mount Yuhak, eight hundred thirty-seven meters high.
To the east, Mount Ka, at nine hundred and two.
The single road between them was the last gate into Taegu.
The ROK 1st Division was commanded by Brigadier General Paik Sun-yup, not yet thirty years old.
His division drew the final line in front of that gate.
s12.name: Paik Sun-yup

lines: Facing him were the North Korean 13th, 1st, and 3rd Divisions.
Tank-led units that had won battle after battle since the invasion began.
The ROK 1st Division, by contrast, had retreated for over a month from the Imjin River, losing much of its men and equipment.
Now its exhausted soldiers faced the heaviest task of all.
s13b.label: ROK soldiers (Sep 1950)

lines: In mid-August, the main assault began.
The North Koreans seized the summit of Mount Yuhak first.
s14.label: The Naktong front (Aug 1950)

lines: For the ROK troops below, the summit was all but impregnable.
Every climb up the rock face was met with a rain of grenades.
s15.label: Dramatization

lines: Shelling by day. Hand-to-hand fighting by night.
Survivors recall that when the ammunition ran out, they fought with bayonets and rocks.
s15b.label: Police who fought at Dabu-dong (Sep 1950)

lines: The heaviest losses fell on Hill 837.
And Hill 328 changed hands fifteen times in twelve days.
On the hilltops, water and rice balls rarely arrived on time.
The ammunition and food that did make it up were carried on the backs of local villagers with wooden A-frames.
s17.label: Dramatization

lines: August 18th.
North Korean shells landed near Taegu Station.
The government relocated to Pusan, and Taegu filled with refugees.
It was, quite literally, the edge of the cliff.
s19.label: Refugees (1950)

lines: Around this time, ROK soldiers defending the hills began abandoning their positions, one by one.
Then the division commander, Paik Sun-yup, stepped forward himself.
s20.label: Dramatization

lines: "We have nowhere left to retreat. If we are pushed back here, we will be driven into the sea."
"If I fall back in fear, then you shoot me."
s21.label: Dramatization
bubbles:
If I fall back,
shoot me!

lines: With their commander charging at the front, the men who had been falling back surged up the hill again.
The crumbling line held once more.
s22.label: Soldiers moving up (Aug 1950)

lines: On the night of August 21st, the ROK 12th Regiment launched a night raid and finally retook Mount Yuhak.
Meanwhile, the road through the valley north of Dabu-dong.
It was held by the U.S. 27th Infantry Regiment, the 'Wolfhounds', committed on August 17th.
Their commander was Colonel John Michaelis.
An elite Eighth Army regiment, rushed like a fire brigade to every crisis on the line.
s24b.label: U.S. 27th Infantry on the Pusan Perimeter (Sep 1950)

lines: ROK troops held the ridges on either side, while American tanks and infantry blocked the valley floor.
At dusk, the Americans laid two belts of mines and trip flares across the road.
Then came the night of August 21st.
Out of the darkness, the roar of tank engines began to rise.
s26.label: Dramatization

lines: The North Korean 13th Division was pushing down the valley, led by T-34 tanks and self-propelled guns.
The American tanks held their fire until the last moment.
When the enemy armor was almost on top of them, they opened up all at once.
s28.label: Dramatization

lines: With the lead tank knocked out, the vehicles behind it were trapped on the narrow road.
In an instant, the valley became a giant trap.
Shells streaking low along the dark valley floor.
To the men watching, it looked like bowling balls rolling toward the pins.
The attacks did not end that night.
For several more nights, the North Koreans came down the same valley.
s29b.label: Dramatization

lines: The fighting raged for nearly five hours.
When dawn broke, only burned-out tanks remained in the valley.
s30.label: Knocked-out North Korean T-34 (Sep 1950)

lines: From August 18th to 25th, U.S. records list North Korean losses as
thirteen T-34 tanks, six self-propelled guns, and twenty-three trucks.
In the same period, American losses were eight killed.
But the ROK troops holding the ridges on both sides lost an estimated two thousand three hundred men.
The North Korean 13th Division lost some three thousand men in this fight alone, and with them, its ability to attack.
s32.label: North Korean POWs (Sep 1950)

lines: Around then, the division's artillery commander, Lieutenant Colonel Jeong Bong-uk, defected to the ROK lines.
A sign that the North Korean army was beginning to crack from within.
s33.label: Lt. Col. Jeong Bong-uk (1950)

lines: So how did Dabu-dong hold for fifty-five days?
Let's break it down into four factors.
s34.head: 8,200 vs 21,000 — How?

lines: First, terrain.
s35.title: Chokepoint Terrain

lines: The narrow valley between Mount Yuhak and Mount Ka was a chokepoint no large army could push through all at once.
In this gorge, the advantage of numbers simply disappeared.
Second, combined ROK-U.S. operations.
s37.title: ROK-U.S. Combined Ops

lines: The ROK held the ridgelines; the Americans held the valley road.
Infantry, armor, and artillery moved as a single, interlocking line of defense.
In this battle, Paik found himself directing the American 27th Regiment at the front as well.
A rare moment: a Korean general in command of a U.S. regiment.
s38b.label: Gen. Paik with U.S. officers (Oct 1950)

lines: Third, firepower.
s39.title: Overwhelming Firepower

lines: On August 16th, ninety-eight B-29 bombers dropped some nine hundred sixty tons of bombs around Waegwan.
In the Bowling Alley fight, a single U.S. artillery battery fired sixteen hundred and sixty-one 105-millimeter rounds.
s40.label: B-29 bombing (1950)

lines: Fourth, the resolve of command.
s41.title: Command Resolve

lines: A unit whose general stands at the very front does not break easily.
And that resolve built trust between Korean and American troops fighting side by side for the first time.
s42.label: Dramatization

lines: According to South Korean records, friendly casualties in this period numbered around ten thousand.
North Korean casualties reached some seventeen thousand five hundred.
Fifty-five desperate days that numbers alone cannot capture.
While Dabu-dong held, the United Nations was preparing its counterstroke.
September 15th, 1950: the Inchon landing.
s45.label: Inchon landing (Sep 15, 1950)

lines: The next day, ROK and UN forces along the Naktong launched a general counteroffensive.
Dabu-dong became the starting line of the breakout.
Today, a war memorial stands at Dabu-dong, honoring that sacrifice every year.
s46b.label: Memorial ceremony at Dabu-dong

lines: Even now, the remains of Korean War dead are still being recovered on Mount Yuhak.
Young men who fell on these ridges, many without even leaving a name.
Most of them were barely twenty.
s48.label: ROK recruits (1950)

lines: And among those who fought on this mountain were villagers who carried A-frames instead of rifles.
s48b.label: Dramatization

lines: The last twenty kilometers to Taegu.
In the end, what held that road was people who refused to step back.
quotes: Held by those who would not step back
